title: Court Strikes Down Trump's $100,000 H-1B Fee as Unlawful Tax, but Stay Keeps It in Effect
excerpt: U.S. District Judge Leo Sorokin vacated the fee imposed by presidential proclamation, calling it an unauthorized tax Congress never approved — but his own temporary stay means employers still must pay while the government appeals.
body:
• A federal judge in Boston ruled June 8 that Trump's $100,000 H-1B visa fee is an unlawful tax that exceeds presidential authority, vacating the policy nationwide.
  • Judge Leo Sorokin cited the Supreme Court's February ruling on tariffs to conclude that immigration law does not delegate Congress's taxing power to the president.
  • Days after the ruling, Sorokin temporarily stayed his own decision, meaning the $100,000 fee remains in effect while the government's appeal moves through the First Circuit.
  • Nearly three-quarters of H-1B approvals go to Indian nationals, making this case one of the most consequential immigration battles for the diaspora.

Judge Calls the Fee a Tax, Not a Penalty

U.S. District Judge Leo Sorokin in Boston delivered a stinging rebuke to the Trump administration on June 8, ruling that the $100,000 fee imposed on new H-1B visa petitions is an unlawful tax that the president had no authority to levy. Sorokin vacated all agency materials implementing the fee, siding with 20 Democratic state attorneys general led by California who challenged the policy.

Trump announced the fee through a presidential proclamation on September 19, 2025, framing it as a penalty to curb what he called "systemic abuse" of the H-1B program. The proclamation prohibited entry under H-1B visas "except for those aliens whose petitions are accompanied or supplemented by a payment of $100,000."

"The substance and application of the $100,000 payment reveal that it is a tax, regardless of what the payment is called."

— Judge Leo Sorokin, U.S. District Court for the District of Massachusetts

Before the proclamation, employers typically paid between $2,000 and $5,000 in fees to sponsor an H-1B worker, depending on company size and other factors. The 20-fold increase effectively priced out schools, hospitals, and smaller employers who depend on the program to fill critical shortages.

Supreme Court Tariff Ruling Guided the Decision

Sorokin anchored his analysis in the Supreme Court's February 2026 decision in Learning Resources v. Trump, which struck down sweeping tariffs the president imposed under emergency powers. In that case, the justices held that the International Emergency Economic Powers Act did not authorize Trump to levy taxes on imports. Sorokin applied the same logic to immigration law.

The Immigration and Nationality Act allows the president to impose "restrictions," "rules," "regulations," "orders," and "limitations" on the entry of noncitizens. But none of those terms, Sorokin wrote, "by their ordinary meaning, include the power to tax." He also found that the fee violated the Administrative Procedure Act because it exceeded the president's statutory authority and was implemented in an "arbitrary and capricious" manner without required notice and comment.

The ruling directly contradicts a December 23, 2025, decision by Judge Beryl Howell in Washington, D.C., who upheld the fee in a separate lawsuit filed by the U.S. Chamber of Commerce. Howell concluded that Congress had delegated sufficiently broad authority to the president to regulate entry, including through monetary requirements.

Fee Remains in Effect During Appeal

The victory for employers proved short-lived. Days after his ruling, Sorokin temporarily stayed his own decision, reinstating USCIS's authority to collect the $100,000 fee for qualifying H-1B petitions involving consular processing. On June 18, the Justice Department formally filed a motion to stay the order for the duration of the appeals process with the First Circuit Court of Appeals.

The White House said it is confident the ruling will be reversed. "President Trump has clear legal authority to restrict entry of any class of aliens he determines is not in America's best interests, and that is exactly what he did," spokeswoman Taylor Rogers said in a statement.

The conflicting rulings between Boston and Washington set up a potential circuit split. The Chamber of Commerce is appealing Howell's ruling to the D.C. Circuit, while a third lawsuit filed in San Francisco by religious groups and labor organizations could produce yet another conflicting decision — raising the prospect that the Supreme Court may ultimately need to resolve the question.

Indian Workers Bear the Brunt

The stakes are especially high for the Indian diaspora. Nearly three-quarters of H-1B visa approvals go to workers from India, according to federal data cited in the case. The program — capped at 65,000 visas annually with an additional 20,000 reserved for holders of advanced degrees — has long been a primary pathway for Indian professionals entering the U.S. workforce in technology, healthcare, and academia.

Court filings revealed the fee's chilling effect on applications. As of February 15, USCIS had received just 85 payments of the $100,000 fee, according to administration data — a fraction of the thousands of petitions the program typically processes. The steep increase forced many employers to abandon or defer sponsorship plans, particularly school districts and universities that lack the budgets of major technology firms.

California employs more teachers on H-1B visas than any state except Texas and North Carolina. During the 2024-25 school year, 294 H-1B visas were granted to California school districts, up from 193 in 2018-19. Major universities including Stanford, the University of Michigan, and the University of Florida each received more than 100 H-1B visa approvals in fiscal 2026.

What Comes Next

The First Circuit will decide whether the fee remains in effect throughout the appeal. If Sorokin's ruling ultimately takes effect, it would apply nationwide, ending the $100,000 requirement for all new H-1B petitions requiring consular processing. The proclamation itself was set to expire in September 2026, but its legal fate could reshape presidential authority over immigration fees for years to come.

For employers and H-1B applicants — a disproportionate number of them Indian nationals — the path forward remains uncertain. The fee is still enforceable, the appeal could take months, and the prospect of divided appellate rulings only adds to the confusion that has gripped the program since September.
